analysis.one_liner: Bars most investors from suing companies for securities fraud in state-court class actions.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 340-83 on July 22, 1998, then set it aside in favor of the Senate's identical bill, which became law that November.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill stops private investors from bringing class actions under state law against companies whose stock is publicly traded, alleging false statements or deceptive practices. Any such state-court case gets moved to federal court, where a 1995 law already makes those suits much harder to win. It keeps a few carve-outs: states and state pension funds can still sue, and claims tied to a company's home-state corporate law survive. It also renews funding for the Securities and Exchange Commission.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies and the people and firms around them — executives, directors, accountants, and underwriters — gain because they can no longer face class-action lawsuits in state courts, where securities claims were often easier for investors to bring and where damages rules varied by state. Companies facing a claim get pulled into federal court, where a 1995 law imposes stricter pleading and stay-of-discovery rules [S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Publicly traded companies and their advisers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any private class action based on state statutory or common law, in state or federal court, alleging a false statement or omission or a deceptive device in the purchase or sale of a covered security [S3][S4].
Allows any such state-court class action to be removed to federal court, where the stricter federal securities-litigation rules apply [S3][S4].
Preserves federal jurisdiction by letting courts stay state-court discovery so plaintiffs cannot work around a federal stay, and reauthorizes SEC funding for fiscal year 1999 [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Investors who bought publicly traded stock — including people whose retirement savings are in it — bear the cost. If a company misleads them, they lose the state-law class action route entirely, and their claims must fit within the federal framework created by the 1995 Private Securities Litigation Reform Act, which many small investors' claims do not clear [S3][S4].

drawbacks.text: Defrauded investors lose access to state courts and state-law protections for claims about publicly traded securities; the bill forecloses class actions in every state court and forces surviving claims into the stricter federal track [S3][S4].

Supporters' good-faith argument: state-court filings were being used to forum-shop and pressure companies into quick settlements of weak claims, raising costs that fell on the same shareholders the suits claimed to protect, and a uniform federal standard ends that. An honest supporter must concede that some investors with real losses will no longer be able to recover at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a large, specific benefit to corporate defendants — the end of parallel state-court litigation — while the cost is spread diffusely among investors, whose ability to recover for losses depends on clearing higher federal hurdles. The carve-outs for state pension plans, states, and issuer-buyback claims soften the blow, but an ordinary 401(k) holder relying on a class action has less recourse than before.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 340-83 under a fast-track procedure that requires two-thirds support, then laid it on the table so the Senate's identical companion, S. 1260, could carry it into law; that bill was enacted in November 1998.

narrative.text: Introduced May 21, 1997 by Rep. Rick White (R-WA) with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors, and referred to the House Committee on Commerce [S6].
The bill attracted 232 cosponsors — 151 Republicans and 81 Democrats — before floor action [S5].
The Commerce subcommittee approved it 21-4 on June 10, 1998, and the full committee ordered it reported as amended by voice vote on June 24 [S6].
On July 22, 1998 the House agreed to suspend the rules and pass the bill 340-83, with Republicans voting 221-2 in favor and Democrats 119-80 [S7].
The House then laid the bill on the table and referred further action to S. 1260, the identical Senate bill, which was enacted in November 1998 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded companies, their executives and directors, and the accounting firms and underwriters that defend securities claims came out ahead; investors lost a route to sue, and state courts lost their role in policing securities fraud.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Publicly traded companies and their executives

sides.party_line_note: Republicans were nearly unanimous (221-2) and Democrats split 119-80 in favor, so the bill passed with heavy bipartisan support but opposition was almost entirely Democratic.

industries.note: The bill eliminates state-law class actions against companies whose stock is publicly traded and moves any remaining claims into federal court under stricter rules. Ordinary investors in those companies — including through retirement accounts — lose a route to recover when a company misleads the market.

industries.industry: Accounting firms, investment banks, and underwriters
industries.note: These firms are frequent co-defendants in securities class actions over false statements and inflated offerings. Preempting state-law claims in state court removes one of the most plaintiff-friendly venues for those suits.

Attorneys who represent defrauded investors lose the ability to file state-law class actions in state courts, which were often faster and more favorable. Their clients' recoveries shrink correspondingly.

industries.industry: State securities regulators and state pension funds
industries.note: The bill expressly preserves state securities commissions' enforcement powers and lets states and state pension plans sue on their own behalf or in classes made up solely of public entities [S3][S4]. But private investors in those states lose state-court access, so public enforcement replaces some private enforcement.

The bill reauthorizes SEC appropriations for fiscal 1999 and requires the agency to report on whether the new preemption helps or hurts investor protection [S3][S4]. The funding secures the agency's role; the reporting requirement acknowledges the preemption could cut against investors.
